definition: A very strict person who demands that rules and orders be followed exactly.
example: The new choir director was a martinet who halted rehearsal whenever a singer came in half a beat late.
nuance: A disciplinarian simply enforces rules; a martinet does so rigidly and over trivial matters, so the word is almost always critical.
prompt: A new supervisor takes over a busy hotel kitchen.
options: The cooks called the new supervisor a martinet because she timed every break to the second.
The new supervisor was such a martinet that she let the cooks wander in at any hour they pleased.
The new supervisor hung a little wooden martinet from strings above the stove.
The cooks praised the martinet for the gentle, flexible way she handled every mistake.
reasons: Enforcing even tiny rules with rigid precision is exactly what earns this label.
Letting staff come and go freely is the reverse of strict control.
This confuses the word with marionette, a puppet moved by strings.
Gentleness and flexibility clash with the harsh rigidity the word conveys.

practice.prompt: A camp counselor runs the morning routine in a cabin of ten-year-olds.
options: Every camper hoped to be named the cabin's martinet, the title for its most cheerful, generous kid.
Known as a martinet, the counselor inspected every bunk and made campers remake any with a wrinkle.
The counselor proved herself a martinet by letting campers skip breakfast and sleep in until noon every day.
The counselor played a cheerful tune on her martinet beside the campfire.
reasons: The term criticizes harsh strictness; it is not a compliment for warmth or kindness.
Demanding perfection over small details marks someone as a rigid enforcer of rules.
Letting the schedule slide completely is the opposite of strict discipline.
The word names a kind of person, not an instrument like a clarinet.
